content.title: Artemis II Splashdown: When To Watch Friday — After 16-Minute Blackout
content.text: ToplineWhat time is splashdown for Artemis II? After an iconic 10-day mission that took the crew of four astronauts around the moon for the first time since 1972, NASA’s Artemis II mission will come to an end on Friday, April 10, when the Orion capsule — named “Integrity” — lands in the Pacific Ocean. However, before splashdown, the crew and the watching world will endure a 16-minute re-entry blackout as Orion’s heat shield heats to 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit as it travels through Earth’s atmosphere. Here’s everything you need to know — and when and where to watch it all live in the U.S. and the U.K. An artist’s impression of the Orion spacecraft with ESA’s service module. NASAKey FactsNASA is targeting 8:07 p.m. EDT (5:07 p.m. PDT) on Friday, April 10 (and 1:07 a.m. BST on Saturday, April 11, for those in the U.K.), for the splashdown of Artemis II in the Pacific Ocean near San Diego. Live coverage on NASA+ begins at 6:30 p.m. EDT (3:30 p.m. PDT/11:30 p.m. BST in the U.K.). Just before re-entry, the Orion capsule will separate from the European Service Module, its life-support system, built by the European Space Agency. After the 16-minute blackout, parachutes will deploy to slow the capsule, and waiting cameras will scan the sky for the first glimpses of “Integrity.” The recovery process is expected to take several hours, with U.S. Navy teams due to secure the Orion capsule and assist the crew aboard the USS John P. Murtha, which departed San Diego on Monday, April 6. The crew will be flown by helicopter to the Murtha for medical evaluations before traveling to Houston.The crew includes Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen. Selected in April 2023, the four astronauts have trained together for three years in preparation for this mission.The astronauts made history at 1:56 p.m. EDT on Monday, April 6, 2026, when they reached 248,655 miles from Earth, the farthest distance ever traveled by humans. It broke a record previously set by Commander Jim Lovell, Command Module Pilot Jack Swigert and Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise during the Apollo 13 mission in 1970. From launch to landing, the Artemis II astronauts will have traveled 695,081 miles.A Fiery Return Through Earth’s AtmosphereBefore splashdown, the Orion spacecraft must endure one of the most intense phases of the mission: atmospheric re-entry. As it descends, temperatures on the heat shield will soar to nearly 5,000°F. During this phase, communications between the spacecraft and Mission Control will be lost for approximately 16 minutes due to a plasma blackout. This occurs when superheated gases surround the capsule, blocking radio signals. A separate, longer communications blackout occurred when the spacecraft passed behind the moon on Monday. It’s the first real-world test of the heat shield since NASA identified minor issues with it after the uncrewed Artemis I mission in 2022. “Atmospheric reentry is one of the most extreme environments any engineered system will face — intense heat, powerful aerodynamic forces, and material degradation all occurring at once,” said Marianna Maiaru, Director of the Guggenheim Initiative for Aerospace Structures at Columbia Engineering, in an email. The Artemis heat shield uses Avcoat, a material that decomposes and releases gases to carry heat away. “For Artemis II, the trajectory has been adjusted to enable a smoother reentry and prevent the behavior observed during Artemis I, but this also changes how the material itself responds, since its behavior is governed by the surrounding thermal and pressure environment,” said Maiaru. The Moon, backlit by the Sun during a solar eclipse, is photographed by NASA’s Orion spacecraft on Monday, April 6, 2026, during the Artemis II mission. Orion is visible in the foreground on the left. Earth is reflecting sunlight at the left edge of the Moon, which is slightly brighter than the rest of the disk. The bright spot visible just below the Moon’s bottom right edge is Saturn. Beyond that, the bright spot at the right edge of the image is Mars.NASA Historic Images And Scientific DiscoveriesDuring their seven-hour flyby of the moon’s far side on Monday, the Artemis II crew captured thousands of images, including views never before seen by human eyes. Among the highlights were a rare in-space solar eclipse, Earthrise and Earthset, and six meteoroid impacts flashing across the lunar surface. They also documented impact craters, ancient lava flows and surface fractures that will help scientists study the moon’s geologic evolution. “Our four Artemis II astronauts — Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy — took humanity on an incredible journey around the Moon and brought back images so exquisite and brimming with science, they will inspire generations to come,” said Dr. Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.The Artemis II crew captured this breathtaking photo of our galaxy, the Milky Way. The Milky Way’s elegant spiral structure is dominated by just two arms wrapping off the ends of a central bar of stars. Spanning more than 100,000 light-years, Earth is located along one of the galaxy’s spiral arms, about halfway from the center.NASANasa’s Artemis Program: What Comes NextNASA’s Artemis program is designed as a step-by-step return to the moon, ultimately culminating in a permanent moon base:Artemis I – Uncrewed test flight that successfully orbited the moon and returned to Earth (completed in 2022)Artemis II – First crewed mission, flying astronauts around the moon (completed 2026)Artemis III – Planned mission to test docking with SpaceX/Blue Origin lunar lander in Earth orbit ahead of a lunar landing (expected 2027)Artemis IV – Expected to deliver astronauts to the moon’s surface, targeting the south pole (expected 2028–2029)Artemis V – A follow-up mission aimed at expanding lunar exploration capabilities (expected 2029–2030)NASA is also planning missions beyond the moon. Recently, NASA announced a nuclear-powered spacecraft — SR-1 Freedom — which is targeted for launch to Mars in 2028. Using nuclear electric propulsion, the mission could dramatically shorten travel times and carry heavier scientific payloads, while deploying advanced robotic helicopters to scout the Martian surface.Further ReadingForbesArtemis Astronauts See Earthrise, Earthset And A Total Solar EclipseForbesNASA Sets 2028 Launch For First Nuclear Mission To Mars Days Before Return To The MoonBy Jamie CarterForbesAnother ‘NASA Eclipse’ Will Hit Kennedy Space Center In 2045By Jamie CarterForbesNASA’s Artemis II Timeline: 8 Key Moments To Watch LiveBy Jamie Carter
